newsitem.title: GERMANY: CDU leader says Kohl pleased with govt, no changes.
newsitem.headline: CDU leader says Kohl pleased with govt, no changes.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl is extremely pleased with the work of his government and has no plans to reshuffle his "winning team", a senior leader in Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) said on Wednesday.

Peter Hintze, general secretary of the CDU, said Kohl saw no need to heed Finance Minister Theo Waigel's calls to replace several ministers now before launching the 1998 election campaign. Waigel leads the CDU's Bavarian sister party, the CSU.

"We have a very successful government team and what applies for sport should also apply for politics -- never change a winning team," Hintze told Berlin's InfoRadio. "The chancellor has said quite clearly this is not the time for a change and he is very pleased with the team he is now leading."

Hintze said in a separate interview with ZDF television that the CDU was unconcerned with opinion surveys showing the centre-right coalition badly trailing a proposed alliance of two left-leaning parties, the Social Democrats and the Greens.
"The CDU has often been down in the opinion polls in midterm years," Hintze said. "But by the time the election arrives the CDU wins back the wide approval of the electorate."

An Emnid Institute survey found voters are losing confidence in Kohl's abilities to resolve urgent economic problems such as unemployment, and for the first time voters no longer view the CDU as the most competent party on business issues.

"The confidence in Kohl has declined most dramatically," said a report on the survey in Wirtschaftswoche business weekly. "Only nine percent view his engagement in fighting unemployment as good while 38 percent say it is deficient."
The magazine said on Wednesday Kohl's ratings were generally poor and well below those of his possible SPD challenger, Lower Saxony premier Gerhard Schroeder.

Christian Wulff, the leader of the CDU in the state of Lower Saxony, said there were too many problems in Germany at the moment to waste time arguing about which ministries will be led by which politicians.

Wulff, one of the so-called "Wild Ones" who dared to publicly criticise Kohl's policies, said the size of the cabinet should be reduced by at least three ministries this year when the post ministry is dissolved.
"Because of the great problems we are facing, some people are inclined to escape into debates about personalities," Wulff told the Berliner Zeitung newspaper.
Franz Muentefering, general secretary of the SPD, said Wulff's remarks showed that Kohl's government was bankrupt.

"The debate in the coalition about the cabinet reshuffle shows that Kohl's government is at the end of its tether," he said. "This government no longer has the stamina needed to resolve the economic and social problems."
A leader of Kohl's junior coalition partners, the FDP, said the three FDP ministers in the government were doing a good job and would not be changed.

"If the CDU and CSU believe that have to fight with each other over the distribution of ministries, then that is their problem," said Guido Westerwelle in an interview with the Ostthueringer Zeitung newspaper.
Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary leader of the CDU, also rejected Waigel's call for a reshuffle and urged the coalition not to be distracted from the important issues of the day.
Schaeuble told the Sueddeutsche Zeitung newspaper that the alliance should focus on pushing through reforms blocked by the opposition SPD in the upper house of parliament.
In a weekend interview, Waigel called on Kohl to replace several ministers in his 17-member cabinet before launching the 1998 election campaign.
